newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: DEMOLITION INQUIRY CRITICISED
The ACT Government has finalised the terms of reference for an independent inquiry into the Royal Canberra Hospital demolition, and has immediately come under fire from the Opposition.
Canberra girl, Katie Bender, aged 12, was killed and several other people were injured by flying debris from the implosion, at the weekend.

Chief Minister Kate Carnell said the terms of reference are broad and although inquiry-head Noel Tanzer will be asked to report by the end of the month, he will be able to continue his inquiry beyond then, if neccessary.

Mr Tanzer will be asked to consider how the decision was made to implode the buildings; the conduct of the tender; safety precuations taken during the implosion and any other matters considered relevant to the contract.
But ACT Opposition leader Andrew Whitecross said the terms of reference are too narrow and limited.

Mr Whitecross said they should include other matters, including an allegation the government influenced the decision-making process in favour of implosion, and who decided the demolition should be a public event.
Federal police have maintained their hotline for information about Sunday's building demolition tragedy.
Police want to hear for anyone who may have suffered injury or property damage, and are still seeking video and still photographs of the incident.
Telephone counselling and referrals are available on the hotline number which is (06) 251 1781.
UNIONS "CAN'T AFFORD" TO ESCALATE HUNTER DISPUTE
The union representing 400 striking miners at the Hunter Valley Number One mine will hold a mass meeting today ahead of another hearing in the Industrial Relations Commission.
ACTU President Jennie George has warned the strike over individual contracts could escalate.
But John Buchanan from the Centre for Industrial Relations at Sydney University has told ABC Radio the union could not afford such action.
Mr Buchanan said the union will be doing its best to ensure the dispute does not spread.
"The new industrial laws are not friendly to multi-employer forms of bargaining or multi-employer forms of industrial action," he said.
"As soon as you escalate the dispute, the unions will find themselves exposed to all kinds of very, very heavy legal penalties and legal sanctions."
HANSON PROTEST PASSES WITHOUT VIOLENCE
Pauline Hanson supporters were outnumbered by protesters and police at last night's One Nation meeting at Werribee, west of Melbourne.
Just over 100 supporters crammed the Werribee West Family Centre, to the jeers and abuse of up to 400 protesters, held back by more than 200 police, including 16 mounted police.
Police were carrying batons, fearing a repeat of last week's violence outside a One Nation meeting in Dandenong, east of Melbourne.
Private security guards were also used and protest groups like Militant used their own marshalls in the crowd.
Police escorted Hanson supporters in and out of the meeting and water-filled barriers kept protesters 10 metres from the building.
Superintendent Bruce Logie says, on the whole, the crowd was well behaved.
At least three eggs were thrown, and some minor scuffles broke out, but police and protest groups praised the crowd, which was noisy, but mostly peaceful.
One Nation's Andrew Carne said the demonstration has created a better environment for Pauline Hanson's appearance at Geelong, west of Melbourne, on Friday.

Meanwhile, a new row has started between the One Nation Party and Militant, over the past of a key anti-Hanson activist. One Nation's Andrew Carne told last night's party gathering Militant's leader, Stephen Jolly, incited student protests at China's Tiananmen Square eight years ago.
But Mr Jolly said he will be talking to his lawyers, describing Mr Carne's claim as an "absolute outrage".
SHIPS TO CARRY ON UP THE REEF
Queensland Transport has confirmed ships will continue to travel inside the Great Barrier Reef despite calls from environmentalists for routes to be changed.
The call comes after the grounding of a bulk carrier in the Torres Strait.

General Manager of Marine Operations John Watkinson said the inner route is still safer than sending ships outside the reef. "The route is extremely well marked. It is compulsory pilotage, it is covered by a $5 million ship reporting system that is established at Hay Point that basically tracks the ship from Torres Strait in the north to south of Hay Point," he said.
